Embryonated eggs of Chum salmon (Oncorhynchus keta) incubating at a stable temperature of 9 °C [T = 9 °C] undergo eclosion after approximately 60 days [ab = approximately 60 days], a developmental timeline that reflects the metabolic constraints of cold-water incubation typical of this species. Upon chorion rupture, the emergent alevins are characterized by a modest initial size, with a total length at birth of 1.6 cm [Lb = 1.6 cm]. This small body dimension at the onset of the yolk-sac stage is accompanied by an equally diminutive wet weight at birth, measured at 0.1575 g [Wwb = 0.1575 g], a value consistent with the species' reproductive strategy of producing numerous but relatively small offspring. The protracted incubation period at 9 °C contrasts with the faster developmental rates observed in salmonids spawning in warmer tributaries, underscoring the significant influence of local thermal regime on early ontogeny.

As the yolk-sac larvae progress through the exotrophic transition, the comparatively brief emergence size provides a challenging energetic baseline for juveniles entering the freshwater rearing environment. Over the course of their first year, the growing parr undergo a period of rapid somatic expansion, yet much of the overall determination of ultimate body dimensions is deferred to the ocean phase. Upon reaching the feeding grounds of the North Pacific, individuals embark on an accelerated growth trajectory that will ultimately define the species' asymptotic size. Field surveys and commercial catch records consistently indicate that the largest recorded individuals reach an ultimate total length of 92 cm [Li = 92 cm], a dimension that marks the upper boundary of somatic growth for the species. This maximum length is complemented by the ultimate wet weight, which can approach 15,900 grams [Wwi = 15,900 grams] in the most robust specimens, a mass that reflects the substantial accumulation of lipid and protein reserves required to sustain a protracted anadromous migration.

Pubertal development in Chum salmon is closely tied to a threshold body length rather than a strict chronological age, with most individuals achieving gonadal maturation upon attaining a total length at puberty of 40 cm [Lp = 40 cm]. This morphological milestone signals the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis and the onset of vitellogenesis in females and spermiation in males. Unlike iteroparous salmonids that may spawn repeatedly, Chum salmon are predominantly semelparous, channeling nearly all available somatic resources into a single, energetically expensive spawning event. The length threshold at puberty is a critical life-history switch, as individuals smaller than this size typically defer reproductive investment for another growing season. Migration toward natal rivers generally commences once this length is achieved, initiating a cessation of feeding and the catabolic mobilization of stored energy reserves for gamete production and the arduous upstream journey.

The total lifespan of Oncorhynchus keta is tightly constrained by its semelparous life cycle, with records of maximum longevity derived from spawning runs in cooler northern rivers. The maximum documented lifespan for this species, observed under natural thermal regimes averaging 7 °C [T = 7 °C], is approximately 7 years [am = approximately 7 years]. This clock is set primarily by the duration of the marine feeding phase, which typically spans three to five years, followed by the terminal freshwater migration. The cooler water temperatures of high-latitude systems prolong metabolic and developmental rates relative to the southern extent of the species' range, thereby contributing to a longer potential pre-spawning interval. The span of 7 years is considerably longer than the lifespan observed in pink salmon, yet shorter than that of the more long-lived Chinook salmon, highlighting the diversity of life-history schedules within the genus Oncorhynchus.

Comparisons across Pacific salmon species reveal how the reproductive investment of Chum salmon is constrained by its semelparous life cycle, with the energetic demands of migration and spawning dictating body size at reproduction. The substantial ultimate wet weight of 15,900 grams [Wwi = 15,900 grams] is largely accumulated during the marine phase, and the rapid loss of condition after river entry illustrates the extreme capital-breeding strategy employed by this species. The timing of the solitary spawning event is coordinated with the completion of gonadal maturation, following the attainment of the 40 cm pubertal size. While the egg size contributes to a modest wet weight at birth of 0.1575 grams [Wwb = 0.1575 grams], the high fecundity exhibited by large females ensures recruitment despite low per-offspring investment. This life-history syndrome—fast growth, early maturation at a fixed size, and a single, fatal spawning act—positions Chum salmon as one of the most specialized anadromous migrants in the Pacific basin.
